 IRS Urges Local Taxpayers to Prepare Now for 2027 Filing Season
 Published: November 20, 2026 at 
 4:10 pm 
 By 
 Vince Ramsey 
 CENTRE – Taxpayers across northeast Alabama and northwest Georgia can take steps now to make next year’s federal tax filing easier.
 In a Nov. 16 reminder , the Internal Revenue Service urged people to organize records, check banking information, and review tax changes.
 The guidance concerns 2026 income tax returns that taxpayers will file in 2027. However, preparing now does not mean filing before all required documents arrive.
 Start a Folder and Add Forms as They Arrive
 The IRS recommends gathering bank routing and account numbers, W-2s from every employer, 1099 forms, and records of digital-asset transactions.
 That includes paperwork from part-time jobs as well as a person’s main employer. In addition, taxpayers should retain records supporting deductions and credits, IRS correspondence, and copies of their previous returns.
 Many year-end income statements will arrive after 2026 ends. Meanwhile, taxpayers can organize existing receipts and identify the employers, banks, and other payers whose forms they expect.
 The IRS says waiting until all tax records arrive helps taxpayers submit accurate returns and avoid errors that could delay refunds.
 Check the Account Used for Your Refund
 The IRS says filing electronically and choosing direct deposit offers the fastest, most secure way to receive a refund.
 In addition, the agency began phasing out paper refund checks in 2025. Taxpayers should therefore confirm their routing and account numbers with their financial institution before filing.
 Some prepaid cards and mobile payment accounts also accept direct deposits. However, taxpayers must confirm that their account supports the service and obtain the correct banking numbers from the provider.
 Refund timing can vary, so families should avoid depending on a refund arriving by a particular date to cover bills.
 Keep Digital-Asset Records, Too
 Residents who use cryptocurrency or other digital assets should also keep transaction records.
 The IRS treats digital assets as property for federal tax purposes. Sales, exchanges, and payments involving these assets can create reporting obligations, even without a tax form from a broker.
 However, simply holding cryptocurrency differs from selling or exchanging it. The IRS provides digital-asset guidance explaining how to answer the return’s digital-asset question and what records to maintain.
 Review Changes and Protect Your Information
 The IRS also encourages taxpayers to review deductions involving qualified tips, qualified overtime compensation, qualified passenger-vehicle loan interest, and seniors.
 Eligibility rules and limits apply, so taxpayers should review current IRS guidance or discuss their circumstances with a qualified preparer.
 An IRS Individual Online Account can provide tax records, available income statements, payment information, and access to an Identity Protection PIN.
 That six-digit PIN helps prevent someone else from filing a federal return using the taxpayer’s identification number. Meanwhile, taxpayers should verify suspicious messages before providing personal or financial information.
 Free Help May Be Available
 The IRS-supported Volunteer Income Tax Assistance and Tax Counseling for the Elderly programs offer free basic return preparation for qualifying taxpayers.
 Services and eligibility vary by location. Residents can use the locator linked on the IRS page or call 800-906-9887 to find assistance.
 The TCE program also focuses particularly on people age 60 and older and retirement-related tax questions.
